1:3.headline: און is the evil act; עמל is its mark on the soul
1:3.body: Malbim says the pair names two things: און is the evil act itself, and עמל is the mark that evil leaves on the soul. Rashi reads און as plunder and violence, and Ibn Ezra says the two words together cover every sin.

sources.quote: יציין באון פעולת הרע בפועל, ובעמל יציין רושם הרע בנפש
sources.says: Malbim says און names the doing of the evil, and עמל names the mark the evil leaves on the soul.

sources.quote: אָוֶן. בִּזָּה וְחָמָס
sources.says: Rashi says און means plunder and violence.

sources.quote: און ועמל הם שם דבר שכולל לכל דבר עון ולכל חטאת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says און and עמל are a name that covers every kind of wrongdoing and sin.

1:6.headline: הנמהר: 'swift', or 'rash and thoughtless'?
1:6.body: Metzudat Zion links הנמהר to מהירות, speed. Radak and Ibn Ezra say it means a people that acts in haste without thinking, like ולבב נמהרים יבין לדעת.

sources.quote: והנמהר. מל׳ מהירות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says הנמהר is from the word for speed.

sources.quote: נמהר במעשיו לא ישכיל מה יעשה וכן ולבב נמהרים יבין לדעת
sources.says: Radak says it means hasty in his deeds, not thinking what he does, as in ולבב נמהרים יבין לדעת.

sources.quote: והנמהר שאין לו מחשבת כהוגן, רק יעשה דברו במהירות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says הנמהר has no proper thought, and does what he says in haste.

1:7.headline: ושאתו: 'his burden of dread', or 'his greatness'?
1:7.body: Rashi hears שאתו as משא, a heavy burden of dread laid on everyone. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion derive it from lifting up, meaning his rank and pride.

sources.quote: הַמְּטִילִין מַשָּׂא וְאֵימָה עַל הַכֹּל
sources.says: Rashi says the kings come from him, laying a burden and dread on everyone.

sources.quote: ושאתו מגזרת נשיאות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שאתו is from the root of lifting up, נשיאות.

sources.quote: מל׳ התנשאות ורוממות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is from rising up and being exalted.

1:9.headline: מגמת פניהם: from 'swallowing', 'facing', or 'longing'?
1:9.body: This word appears once. Rashi ties it to הגמיאיני, 'let me swallow', so their eager faces seem to swallow the ground ahead. Ibn Ezra says it can also mean 'toward', like נגד ונכח. Metzudat Zion says it is thought and desire, with no parallel.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ״הַגְמִיאִינִי נָא״ (בראשית כד:יז), ״יְגַמֶּא אָרֶץ״ (איוב לט:כד)
sources.says: Rashi says it is from the word in הגמיאיני נא and יגמא ארץ, which means to swallow.

sources.quote: הוא כמו נגד ונכח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like נגד and נכח, 'opposite' and 'facing'.

sources.quote: ענין המחשבה והחשק ואין לו דומה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is about thought and desire, and has no parallel.

1:9.headline: קדימה: 'eastward', or 'like the east wind'?
1:9.body: Ibn Ezra says קדימה is hard, because the Chaldeans come from the east. Radak adds that on reaching Israel their faces point west. Rashi reads it as the east wind, the strongest of the winds, a picture of their fierce faces.

sources.quote: ומלת קדימה קשה, כי מפאת מזרחה בא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word קדימה is difficult, because the Chaldeans come from the east.

sources.quote: והנה לא היה נכח פניהם מזרח אלא מערב
sources.says: Radak says their faces were not toward the east, but toward the west.

sources.quote: דּוֹמֶה לְרוּחַ הַקָּדִים עַזָּה שֶׁבָּרוּחוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it is like the east wind, the fiercest of the winds.

1:10.headline: יתקלס: talk about someone, for good or bad
1:10.body: Rashi says every use of the root קלס is a word for talk about someone, and it can be good or bad. Here it means he mocks kings. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say it means mockery, like לקלס אתנן in Ezekiel.

sources.quote: וְכָל לְשׁוֹן ׳קַלָּסָה׳ לְשׁוֹן ׳דִּבּוּר׳ הַנִּדְבָּרִים בּוֹ, יֵשׁ לְטוֹב יֵשׁ לְרַע
sources.says: Rashi says every use of the word קלסה is about speech that people say about someone, sometimes for good and sometimes for bad.

sources.quote: מגזרת לעג וקלס וכמוהו לקלס אתנן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is from the root of mockery and scorn, like לקלס אתנן.

sources.quote: ענין לעג והתול כמו לקלס אתנן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means mockery and jeering, like לקלס אתנן in Ezekiel.

1:13.headline: צדיק ממנו: 'more righteous than he', not a fully righteous man
1:13.body: The verse says the wicked swallows one 'more righteous than he'. Radak quotes the sages: a man only more righteous than him gets swallowed, a fully righteous man does not. Rashi says the righteous one is Zedekiah, whose eyes Nebuchadnezzar put out.

sources.quote: צדיק ממנו בולע צדיק גמור אין בולע
sources.says: Radak quotes the sages that one more righteous than him is swallowed, but a fully righteous man is not.

sources.quote: כי אין בדרך האמת לבלע רשע צדיק ממנו ואם לא יהיה צדיק גמור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is not the way of truth for a wicked man to swallow one more righteous than he, even if the man is not fully righteous.

sources.quote: צַדִּיק מִמֶּנּוּ. שֶׁהוּא מְסַמֵּא אֶת עֵינֵי צִדְקִיָּהוּ
sources.says: Rashi says the one 'more righteous than he' is Zedekiah, whose eyes he blinds.

1:16.headline: חרמו, the king's net, also sounds like חרם, a banned idol
1:16.body: The Chaldean 'sacrifices to his net'. Metzudat David says the Torah calls idols חרם, a banned thing, so the prophet chose that word for the net as a play on words. Rashi says it means he sacrifices to an idol that, he says, conquers everything for him.

sources.quote: ולפי שנא׳ בעכו״ם שקץ וגו׳ כי חרם הוא (דברים ז) לכן אחז לשון חרם לצחות המליצה
sources.says: Metzudat David says that because the Torah says of idols 'it is a חרם', the prophet took the word חרם for the sake of a witty phrase.

sources.quote: לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁהוּא אוֹמֵר שֶׁהִיא כּוֹבֶשֶׁת הַכֹּל לְפָנָיו
sources.says: Rashi says he sacrifices to idol worship, which he says conquers everything before him.

2:1.headline: The sages saw a circle drawn on the ground here
2:1.body: Plainly, מצור is a siege: the prophet is like a besieged man with no way out of his question. Rashi and the sages read it as a circle Habakkuk drew and stood inside, refusing to leave until God answered.

sources.quote: עָג עוּגָה חֲבַקּוּק וְעָמַד בְּתוֹכָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says Habakkuk drew a circle and stood inside it.

sources.quote: מצור כאדם שצרים עליו ואין לו מנוס
sources.says: Radak says the prophet is like a man under siege with no escape from his confusion.

sources.quote: ורבותינו פירשו מה שאמר על מצור שעג עוגה ועמד בתוכה
sources.says: Radak adds that the sages explained 'on the siege' as the circle he drew and stood in.

2:2.headline: 'Write the vision', or 'the vision is already written'
2:2.body: God tells Habakkuk כתב, write. The Aramaic translation reads it as 'it is written', meaning written in the Torah. Rashi explains: the vision is already in the Torah but hidden, and Habakkuk must spell it out.

sources.quote: כְּתִיבָא נְבוּאֲתָא וּמְפָרְשָׁא עַל סִפְרָא דְאוֹרַיְתָא
sources.says: The Aramaic translation says the prophecy is written and explained in the book of the Torah.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם ״כְּתֹב״ כְּמוֹ ״כְּתִיב״
sources.says: Rashi notes that the translation takes 'write' as 'it is written'.

sources.quote: כְּבָר כָּתוּב חָזוֹן בַּתּוֹרָה, אֲבָל סָתוּם הוּא. הוֹסִיף אַתָּה וּבָאֵר עַל הַלּוּחוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says God told Habakkuk the vision is already in the Torah but hidden, and he should add to it and explain it on tablets.

2:3.headline: A word for breath used to mean speech
2:3.body: ויפח comes from the word for breathing out. Rashi says speech is only breath from the mouth, so the Bible can call it breath. Malbim says the word means speech that is not complete, a hint rather than a plain statement.

sources.quote: וְעַל שֵׁם שֶׁהַדִּבּוּר אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא רוּחַ הַיּוֹצֵא מִן הַפֶּה, קוֹרֵהוּ ׳פִּיחַ׳
sources.says: Rashi says speech is only breath leaving the mouth, so it is called by a word for breath.

sources.quote: מורה על הדיבור הבלתי נשלם
sources.says: Malbim says the word means speech that is not complete.

2:3.headline: It may be slow, yet still not late
2:3.body: The verse says 'if it tarries, wait; it will not be late'. Malbim says these are two different things. A thing set for a thousand years that comes on time is slow but not late.

sources.quote: ויש מתמהמה ובלתי מתאחר, אם נקבע הזמן לאלף שנה ובא בעתה
sources.says: Malbim says something can be slow without being late, if it was set for a thousand years and comes on time.

sources.quote: חַכֵּה לוֹ כִּי לֹא יְאַחֵר אַחַר הַשִּׁבְעִים כְּלוּם
sources.says: Rashi says to wait for it, for it will not come even a little after the seventy years.

2:4.headline: A one-time word: swollen with pride, or hiding in a fort
2:4.body: עפלה appears only here. Rashi reads it as brazen pride, like the Israelites who pushed up the mountain. Radak's brother links it to עופל, a high fortress: the soul hides in a stronghold instead of turning to God.

sources.quote: עֻפְּלָה לְשׁוֹן ׳עַזּוּת׳
sources.says: Rashi says עפלה means brazenness.

sources.quote: ורבי אחי רבי משה ז"ל פירש הנה עפלה מן עופל ובחן שהוא מבצר גבוה
sources.says: Radak brings his brother Rabbi Moshe, who derived the word from עופל, a high fortress.

sources.quote: הנפש הבלתי ישרה תתנשא לעלות למעלה ממדרגתה
sources.says: Malbim says a crooked soul pushes to climb above its rank.

2:5.headline: Does the wine betray, or the drinker?
2:5.body: Rashi reads it literally: the king's own wine betrays him, as at Belshazzar's feast in Daniel. Radak and Metzudat Zion read היין as 'the wine man', the drunkard who is himself treacherous.

sources.quote: שֶׁיִּבְגֹּד בּוֹ יֵינוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says his wine will betray him.

sources.quote: איש היין וכן לץ היין
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means the man of wine, as in 'wine is a mocker'.

sources.quote: שותה היין וכן לץ היין
sources.says: Radak says it means the one who drinks wine.

2:6.headline: One word heard as two: 'thick mud'
2:6.body: עבטיט appears only here. Metzudat Zion and Radak split it into עב טיט, a thick load of mud: his loot weighs on him like clay. Malbim takes it from עבט, a pledge, so he loads himself with debts.

sources.quote: כמו עב טיט ר״ל משא עבה של טיט
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like עב טיט, a thick load of mud.

sources.quote: עבטיט מלה אחת ופירושה כשתי מלות עבטיט כמו טיט עב
sources.says: Radak says it is one word that means two words: thick mud.

sources.quote: מענין והעבטת גוים רבים, ושרשו עבט
sources.says: Malbim says the root is עבט, as in lending on pledge to many nations.

2:7.headline: Those who bite you, or those you owe interest?
2:7.body: נשך means to bite, and it is also the word for interest on a loan. Radak reads 'those who bite you' as the worms in the grave. Malbim reads them as creditors rising up to collect the interest.

sources.quote: ויקומו פתע נושכיך והם התולעים
sources.says: Radak says those who suddenly rise to bite him are the worms.

sources.quote: נשכיך. מלשון לא תשיך לאחיך
sources.says: Malbim says the word comes from 'you shall not lend at interest to your brother'.

sources.quote: הלא יקומו לוקחי הנשך והתרבית ויתבעו ממך תשלומי הנשך שחייבת
sources.says: Malbim says the lenders will rise and demand the interest he owes.

2:10.headline: Cutting off nations, or the ends of the nations?
2:10.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read קצות as a verb: to strip or cut off many peoples. Ibn Ezra offers a reading he prefers, the noun 'ends': shame for your house from all the ends of the nations.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן שְׁלִיפָה וְקִלּוּף, כְּמוֹ ״הִקְצוֹת אֶת הַבַּיִת״
sources.says: Rashi says it means stripping and peeling, as in scraping a house.

sources.quote: ענין חתוך וכריתה כמו וקצותה את כפה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means cutting off.

sources.quote: פירוש אחר ונכון הוא: להיותו דבק אל בושת מכל קצות העמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra gives another reading he calls correct: shame from all the ends of the nations.

2:10.headline: Here 'sinning' means losing
2:10.body: חטא usually means to sin. Metzudat Zion reads it as lacking or losing, as when Bathsheba says she and Solomon will be חטאים, the losers. Rashi: he forfeits his own life.

sources.quote: ענין חסרון כמו והייתי אני ובני שלמה חטאים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means lack, as in 'I and my son Solomon will be חטאים'.

sources.quote: חוֹטֵא לְאַבֵּד נַפְשׁוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means to lose his life.

2:13.headline: Toiling for a great fire, or just enough for fire
2:13.body: The peoples toil בדי אש. Metzudat Zion and Radak say די here means much: they toil for a great fire. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'enough for': all their work is just enough to feed the fire.

sources.quote: בדי אש. בהרבה אש וכן בדי ריק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means with much fire.

sources.quote: ומלת די נוספת בהם מורה על התמדת הדבר והגדלתו
sources.says: Radak says the added word די shows that the thing goes on and grows.

sources.quote: ומלת בדי כמו יספיק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בדי means 'it suffices'.

2:15.headline: Your anger, or your wineskin?
2:15.body: חמתך can mean 'your fury' or 'your skin bottle', as Hagar's water skin in Genesis. Ibn Ezra reads it as the wineskin the king pours from. Radak prefers 'your fury'.

sources.quote: והטעם שאתה מספח מלכים להשקותם חמתך, כמו חמת מים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the king gathers kings to give them drink from his skin bottle, like a water skin.

sources.quote: ויותר נכון לפרש חמתך כמשמעו מן אף וחמה
sources.says: Radak says it is better to read it in its plain sense, as anger and fury.

2:15.headline: A one-time word: their nakedness, or their vomit?
2:15.body: מעוריהם appears only here. Rashi and Radak read it as nakedness, like Noah when drunk. Malbim links it to a verb for pouring out, so the king watches the drunk kings throw up.

sources.quote: כמו ערותם אף על פי שהם שני שרשים
sources.says: Radak says it means their nakedness, though the two words come from different roots.

sources.quote: לְהִגָּלוֹת קְלוֹנָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means to expose their shame.

sources.quote: מענין תשכרי ותתערי, שיוצק מה ששתה ומקיאו
sources.says: Malbim says it is like 'you will be drunk and pour out', meaning he pours out what he drank and vomits.

2:16.headline: Be stopped up, be exposed, or drink poison?
2:16.body: Rashi reads הערל as 'be blocked', since ערלה means a covering that shuts. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'let your foreskin show', disgraced like the kings you made drunk. Malbim swaps two letters and hears רעל, poison.

sources.quote: כָּל עָרְלָה לְשׁוֹן ׳אֹטֶם׳ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says every ערלה in the Bible means being blocked.

sources.quote: והטעם: תראה ערלתך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meaning is that your foreskin will be seen.

sources.quote: תמלא רעל, כמו כבש כשב
sources.says: Malbim says it means you will be filled with poison, with letters swapped as in כבש and כשב.

2:16.headline: Two words fused: vomit and shame
2:16.body: קיקלון appears only here. Radak says it joins קיא, vomit, and קלון, shame. Metzudat David says vomit fits because the punishment is pictured as a cup that makes the king drunk.

sources.quote: קיקלון מלה מורכבת מן קיא וקלון רוצה לומר קיא של קלון
sources.says: Radak says קיקלון is built from vomit and shame, meaning the vomit of shame.

sources.quote: ולפי שהמשיל הפורענות לשתיית היין אמר לשון קיא כי דרך השכור להקיא
sources.says: Metzudat David says the verse says vomit because it pictures the punishment as drinking wine, and drunks vomit.

2:17.headline: Lebanon stands for the Temple, or for the land
2:17.body: Rashi follows the Aramaic and reads 'Lebanon' as the Temple. Metzudat Zion reads it as the Land of Israel. Ibn Ezra keeps it literal: the trees of Lebanon cut down for Babylon's buildings.

sources.quote: חֲמַס לְבָנוֹן. בֵּית מַקְדְּשָׁא
sources.says: Rashi says the violence done to Lebanon means the Temple.

sources.quote: כן נקרא א״י כמ״ש ההר הטוב הזה והלבנון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the Land of Israel is called Lebanon, as in Moses' 'this good mountain and the Lebanon'.

sources.quote: הטעם שכרתה עצי הלבנון לבנייך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means you cut down the trees of Lebanon for your buildings.

3:2.headline: 'Remember mercy': in a midrash, רחם adds up to Abraham
3:2.body: Plainly, the prophet asks God to remember mercy even in anger. Radak brings a midrash: the letters of רחם add up to the same number as אברהם, 248. So the plea also means 'remember Abraham's covenant'.

sources.quote: ודרך הדרש רח"ם בגימטריא אברהם חשבון זה כזה כלומר זכור להם ברית אברהם
sources.says: Radak says that by way of midrash, רחם has the same number value as אברהם, meaning 'remember Abraham's covenant for them'.

sources.quote: רחם תזכור רחמיך ומלת רחם לשון יחיד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'remember Your mercies', and רחם is the singular form.

3:3.headline: From Teman: Edom, 'the south', or Esau who refused the Torah
3:3.body: Metzudat Zion says Teman is the land of Edom, south of Israel. The Aramaic translation says simply 'from the south'. Rashi reads it through a midrash: God went first to Esau and Ishmael with the Torah, and they would not take it.

sources.quote: מתימן. הוא ארץ אדום שהוא בדרומה של א״י
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says Teman is the land of Edom, in the south of the Land of Israel.

sources.quote: וי"ת מתימן מדרומא
sources.says: Radak notes the Aramaic translation renders it 'from the south'.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁבָּאתָ לִתֵּן אֶת הַתּוֹרָה, חָזַרְתָּ עַל עֵשָׂו וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל וְלֹא קִבְּלוּהָ
sources.says: Rashi says that when God came to give the Torah He went round to Esau and Ishmael, and they did not accept it.

3:3.headline: סלה: 'forever', or a sign to pause?
3:3.body: Radak notes that סלה appears in the Bible only in this prayer and in Psalms. Metzudat Zion says it means 'forever'. Malbim says it marks a break, where one idea ends and another begins.

sources.quote: ואינה כתובה זאת המלה בכל המקרא כי אם בזאת התפלה ובספר תהילים
sources.says: Radak says the word is written nowhere in Scripture except in this prayer and in Psalms.

sources.quote: סלה. לעולם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says סלה means 'forever'.

sources.quote: סלה. מלה זאת תציין ההפסק
sources.says: Malbim says this word marks a break.

3:3.headline: His praise fills the earth, or His shining light?
3:3.body: Maimonides reads תהלה as praise. He says this verse means the same as 'the whole earth is full of His glory', since praise is also called glory. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as shining, from Job's 'when His lamp shone (בהלו) over my head'.

sources.quote: בשווה למה שנאמר "וּתְהִלָּתוֹ מָלְאָה הָאָרֶץ" (חבקוק ג,ג). כי השיבוח נקרא כבוד
sources.says: Maimonides says 'the whole earth is full of His glory' matches 'His praise fills the earth', because praise is called glory.

sources.quote: ותהלתו. זהרו מן בהלו נרו עלי ראשי
sources.says: Radak says it means His brightness, from 'when His lamp shone over my head'.

sources.quote: ותהלתו. ענין הארה וזוהר כמו בהלו נרו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means light and brightness.

3:5.headline: Burning coals, a burning fever, or fiery angels?
3:5.body: Metzudat Zion reads רשף as burning coals, as in Song of Songs. Radak reads it as a burning fever that kills fast. Rashi says angels of fire came with God to Sinai.

sources.quote: רשף. גחלי אש כמו רשפיה רשפי אש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רשף means coals of fire.

sources.quote: והוא חולי הקדחת שהיא חמה השורפת וממיתה מהרה
sources.says: Radak says it is the fever sickness, which burns hot and kills quickly.

sources.quote: מַלְאֲכֵי רֶשֶׁף בָּאוּ עִמּוֹ לְסִינַי
sources.says: Rashi says angels of רשף came with Him to Sinai.

3:9.headline: Your bow laid bare: two roots that both mean 'uncover'
3:9.body: Rashi reads both words as uncovering: God's strength was shown in the open. Radak says עריה and תעור come from two different roots that both mean to lay bare. Ibn Ezra sees the bow as the rainbow in the cloud on a rainy day.

sources.quote: עֶרְיָה תֵעוֹר קַשְׁתֶּךָ. נִגְלֹה נִגְלֵית גְּבוּרָתְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says it means Your strength was fully revealed.

sources.quote: ותעור גם כן ענין גלוי אלא שאינו משרשו
sources.says: Radak says תעור also means uncovering, though it is not from the same root.

sources.quote: ותעור תגלה הקשת וזאת כמראה הקשת אשר יהיה בענן ביום הגשם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the bow is uncovered, like the bow seen in the cloud on a day of rain.

3:14.headline: You pierced, or You pronounced a decree?
3:14.body: Metzudat Zion reads נקבת as piercing, from נקב, a hole. Malbim reads it as speaking clearly and decreeing, as in 'which the mouth of the LORD will name (יקבנו)'.

sources.quote: נקבת. מל׳ נקב וחור
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from נקב, a hole.

sources.quote: נקבת. ענינו דיבור מפורש וגזרה חרוצה, כמו אשר פי ה' יקבנו
sources.says: Malbim says it means clear speech and a firm decree, as in 'which the mouth of the LORD will name'.

3:15.headline: Heaps of water, or water churning and foaming?
3:15.body: Rashi follows the Aramaic: the sea stood in heaps, as the frogs lay in 'heaps upon heaps'. Radak says the waters stood up like a wall. Malbim also suggests churning, as in 'its waters roar and foam'.

sources.quote: חֹמֶר. תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: בְּדִגּוּר. לְשׁוֹן ״חֳמָרִים חֳמָרִים
sources.says: Rashi says the Aramaic renders it 'in a heap', as in 'heaps upon heaps'.

sources.quote: חומר מים רבים. כמו שאמר נצבו כמו נד נוזלים
sources.says: Radak says it is like 'the waters stood up like a wall'.

sources.quote: חמר. כמו יהמו יחמרו מימיו, שהמים מעלים רתיחות
sources.says: Malbim says it is like 'its waters roar and foam', when water boils up.

3:16.headline: Lips that rattled like bells and cymbals
3:16.body: Rashi ties צללו to the bells on a horse, and Ibn Ezra to cymbals. The prophet's lips knocked together from fear, so loudly you could hear them.

sources.quote: עַד שֶׁשְּׂפָתַי נוֹקְשׁוֹת זוֹ לָזוֹ וְקוֹלוֹ נִשְׁמָע
sources.says: Rashi says his lips knocked against each other until the sound could be heard.

sources.quote: צָלְלוּ. לְשׁוֹן ״מְצִילּוֹת הַסּוּס
sources.says: Rashi says the word is like 'the bells of the horse'.

sources.quote: צללו שפתי שתכה זאת את זאת מגזרת מצלתים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the lips strike each other, from the word for cymbals.

3:16.headline: Rest, or stand firm? Maimonides reads 'stay fixed'
3:16.body: Radak reads אנוח as 'rest': the prophet hoped for rest at home, and it turned into a day of trouble. Maimonides says the root נוח can also mean to be set in place and stay fixed, and reads this verse that way.

sources.quote: אשר הייתי חושב שאנוח בארצי אחר ששבתי מהגלות לארצי והנה נהפכה מנוחתי ליום צרה
sources.says: Radak says he thought he would rest in his land after returning from exile, and his rest became a day of trouble.

sources.quote: וכבר מצאנו גם בשורש הזה של נחי העי"ן (=שורש נו"ח) משמעות של שימה וייצוב
sources.says: Maimonides says the root נוח also has the sense of placing and setting firm.

sources.quote: ובמשמעות הזו גם כן לדעתי: "אֲשֶׁר אָנוּחַ לְיוֹם צָרָה
sources.says: He says this verse uses the word in that sense.
